Although this should have been implemented in HTTPClient calls instead of HTTPRequest, i realized that halfway through. I can rewrite it for HTTPClient instead if desired.
Also, timeout could have been a parameter for the request() method instead of a property but i figured out that there is no reason setting the timeout for each request.

**EDIT:** A custom response code should be added for this one? Like RESPONSE_CUSTOM_TIMEOUT since its not a standard socket error, we are forcefully closing the connection after the timeout is reached.
@Faless please review.

This should close #30276

I think this probably needs to go into `StreamPeerTCP`.

EDIT: Of course, there you can't use timers, but need to use the OS timing function during poll (`OS::get_singleton()->get_ticks_msec()`).

@zaksnet well, I would say we need to first define what problem we are trying to solve.
And please bear with me because I'm still trying to wrap my mind about this.

If I understand the problem correctly, windows does not seem to timeout during the connection phase, but it does timeout correctly an already established connection. So, we should only check for timeout "manually" during the TCP `connect` phase to at least normalize behaviour across OSes.
Timing out an HTTP connection where data is flowing is another matter, and while it's an interesting point, you might probably want a separate timeout value for that. You need to take into account how much data you need to transfer, how good the user connection is, etc.

So, this PR do cover the second problem, and it might be okay. But I don't think it solves the underlying one for which we probably need another PR. That said, this one is good enough for the "request is taking too long" use case, I'll go on and review it.

>Timing out an HTTP connection where data is flowing is another matter, and while it's an interesting point, you might probably want a separate timeout value for that. You need to take into account how much data you need to transfer, how good the user connection is, etc.

@Faless Sorry my fault, i only want to timeout a connection when the status is `connecting` and not when it is `connected` (because as you pointed out, it times out correctly while connected). I just forgot to cancel the timer when the status changes to `connected` 😳 . In my use case, even if the timeout worked as expected and dropped the connection after 5, 8, 10 min it would still not be enough, I'd need a much smaller number (something like 20 sec).

>If I understand the problem correctly, windows does not seem to timeout during the connection phase, but it does timeout correctly an already established connection. So, we should only check for timeout "manually" during the TCP connect phase to at least normalize behaviour across OSes.

Correct me if i'm wrong but i think what you want is to normalize timeout across platforms internally so i assume there will be no setter/getter, the connection will be dropped after a fixed `timeout`. Although i understand the use case for this, I'm afraid it would not fit my needs.

Canceling the timer once a connection is established would be enough to please my needs, but as you said it will not fix the root problem.

~~(This is in general for sockets, not just http):
Also, a timeout message could be useful as it could be used to `ping` idle connections (or to send any other message to idle clients). This is for already established connections.~~ nvm that, irrelevant with the current thread.

@Faless ,or maybe have 2 timeout enums. One for while connecting and one while connected. RESULT_TIMEOUT_WHILE_CONNECTING and RESULT_TIMEOUT to be more explicit. But the timeout should reset every time we receive data.

**EDIT:** The way I'm thinking about timeout is "While the connection is idle (no actions issued or data transferred) and not as a strict timeout that will drop the connection after `x` amount of time no matter what.

Another commit was pushed that i feel will fit everyone's needs. 
Instead of forcefully closing the connection on timeout, we can emit a "timeout" signal. Users can take that signal and do whatever they want with it, some might want to close the connection, others might want to load another link (in case this one was broken), others might want to reset the timeout for another `x` seconds. Also, the signal will emit the most useful info (instead of empty arrays and strings, which is what a failed request_complete emitted), the host, port, url body and status.

So with this, in my use case, i can just check the status and if its 3 (still trying to connect) then i can close the connection.

My thoughts about this:

- Timeout should affect the whole request, not just the connect part. for that, #30422 is IMO a better fix.
- Timeout should close the connection, no point in emitting signal and forcing the user to still write code for it.
- Timeout should be the maximum time the dev expects the `HTTPRequest` will take before completion. I.e. no matter if partial data is transmitted, if that amount of time has elapsed, the request will stop.

> My thoughts about this:
> 
> * Timeout should affect the whole request, not just the connect part. for that, #30422 is IMO a better fix.
> * Timeout should close the connection, no point in emitting signal and forcing the user to still write code for it.
> * Timeout should be the maximum time the dev expects the `HTTPRequest` will take before completion. I.e. no matter if partial data is transmitted, if that amount of time has elapsed, the request will stop.

Alright, here is why i switched to a signal instead:
First of all, I changed the logic of the timeout, it no longer occurs only when the `connecting` part happens. It will occur after the specified amount of time no matter what the connection state is. For that reason, this PR does not conflict with #30422 .
- A signal is better because you can use coding logic in there, like checking for broken links and loading new ones from a list.
- You can check the state of the connection and the url and either reset the timeout or close the connection.
- The user will probably only have to write 1 line of code in case all they want is to close the connection on timeout.
- You can use the signal to yield.

EDIT: Plus signals are a much better way of handling anything. Gives more freedom.

>     * A signal is better because you can use coding logic in there, like checking for broken links and loading new ones from a list.

You can do that when you get the request done signal with result = timeout error.

>     * You can check the state of the connection and the url and either reset the timeout or close the connection.

Do you have a use case for that? Can't you, in that rare case simply raise the timeout and make the request again? What would the difference be?

>     * The user will probably only have to write 1 line of code in case all they want is to close the connection on timeout.

Yeah, so for very common cases we would require you to write code, just because we want to make very rare cases slightly easier. It doesn't seem like a good idea for me.
@Faless , I'll do some testing with the fix you provided in #30422 and come back to this.
I still feel the timeout signal would be handy, for the same reason HTTPRequest exists (and many other classes), to simplify things. That said, @Faless , i'v made all the changes you requested.

issue_context.body:

**Godot version:**
v.3.1.stable.official


**OS/device including version:**
Windows 10


**Issue description:**
Connection never times out when connecting with a host that does not exist. I think it only happens when trying to connect with ip hosts, status is indefinitely `STATUS_CONNECTING` (3). I'm not sure if that is expected behavior so for now i'v created a `Timer` `Node` and i cancel the request on timeout of the timer.
What i was expecting is the request to timeout at some point and call the `request_complete` signal. Also i was expecting to find out some `timeout` property or parameter in case we need to timeout the connection manualy.

**Steps to reproduce:**
Request anything from an unrelovable ip, example:
```
request("http://10.10.10.10:1234"
request("http://127.0.0.1:1234"
request("http://1.1.1.1:1234"
```
Any of these should be able to reproduce it as long as there is no server running on these ips/ports.
comments:
If really the server is not responding, it should time out, but the timeout is 5 minutes.

Are you sure it doesn't timeout after 5 minutes? I tested it, and for me it times out after 5 minutes as it should.

`request("http://127.0.0.1:1234")` should btw fail immediately, because unless you have a firewall active on localhost you will get a connection refused.

You don't get it for external server servers because most of them have firewall set on [`DROP` and not `REJECT`](https://serverfault.com/questions/157375/reject-vs-drop-when-using-iptables).

If the IP does not exists (which for IPv4 is very unlikely now, unless it's a private address) you'll probably get disconnected very soon too, since routers will send back to your machine a "destination unreachable" packet.

That said, I agree, we should add an option to specify a TCP timeout different from the default `300` seconds.

review_comments:
We need to stop the timer if the request completes correctly, or two `request_completed` will be fired, the first one succeeding, the second one failing.
The timer should also be stopped if the user cancels the request manually.
Timer should be set to one_shot, or it will keep firing after being started the first time.
